```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmt_e <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
count_of <- function(tab, j) sum(tab$judgement == j)
```

## Model

Gould and Wang (2017) use external information about the event rate in
patients not receiving the test product to judge whether the blinded total
event count \(X\) is higher than expected. With \(N\) subjects,
\(N_d = \mathrm{round}(k N / (k + 1))\) on study drug and \(N_c = N - N_d\)
on control (the expected arm sizes), \(X\) is the sum of
\(\mathrm{Binomial}(N_d, p_d)\) and \(\mathrm{Binomial}(N_c, p_c)\) counts.
The control probability has an informative Beta prior, and the metric of
the difference (the ratio \(R = p_d / p_c\), the difference, or the odds
ratio) has a diffuse prior: for the ratio, a lognormal distribution with
mean 1 and probability 0.95 between 0.1 and 10, truncated to
\(R \le 1 / p_c\). For large trials and rare events, a Poisson likelihood
with a Gamma prior of the control rate is used instead. `canary_post()`
integrates the two-dimensional posterior (one-dimensional for the Poisson
likelihood) numerically.

```{r fit}
canary_post(y = 12, n = 100, k = 1, prior_c = c(1, 49))
canary_post(y = 12, n = 100, k = 1, prior_c = c(1, 49),
            metric = "difference")
```

## Decision rules and their operating characteristics

Over the range of counts that matters for monitoring, the posterior
probability increases with the event count, so a rule
"\(P(R > R_\mathrm{crit} \mid X) > \gamma_\mathrm{crit}\)" is equivalent to
\(X \ge X_\mathrm{crit}\). (For counts close to \(N\), both event
probabilities must be close to 1, and the probability of a large ratio falls
again; `signal_count()` therefore searches upward from 0.) `signal_count()`
finds \(X_\mathrm{crit}\) for each sample size (the control charts of
Figure 2), and `count_oc()` gives
the exact probability of reaching it under true event rates (Figure 3 and
Table V).

```{r rule}
sc <- signal_count(n = c(100, 200, 500), method = "canary",
                   prior_c = c(20, 980), crit = 2, cutoff = 0.8)
sc
count_oc(sc$y_crit, sc$n, rate_c = 0.02, rate_d = 0.08)
```

## Reproduction of Gould and Wang (2017)

```{r repro, include = FALSE}
g <- read_results("reproduce", "reproduce_Gould2017.csv")
t1 <- g[grepl("^G_T1", g$id), ]
t3 <- g[grepl("^G_T3", g$id), ]
t5x <- g[grepl("^G_T5_X", g$id), ]
t5p <- g[grepl("^G_T5_P", g$id), ]
a <- read_results("validation", "validate_gould2017_author_grid.csv")
ac <- read_results("validation", "gould2017_author_code.csv")
```

`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Gould2017.R` compares

* the `r nrow(t1)` prior parameters of Table I, from `elicit_prior()`:
  `r count_of(t1, "PASS")` PASS;
* the `r nrow(t3)` critical counts of Table III (binomial likelihood):
  `r count_of(t3, "PASS")` PASS and `r count_of(t3, "EXPLAINED")` EXPLAINED;
* the `r nrow(t5x)` critical counts of Table V (Poisson likelihood):
  `r count_of(t5x, "PASS")` PASS and `r count_of(t5x, "EXPLAINED")`
  EXPLAINED;
* the `r nrow(t5p)` probabilities of Table V, from `count_oc()`:
  `r count_of(t5p, "PASS")` PASS.

The published critical counts were computed by the authors' R code on fixed
grids. A transcription of the code, kept outside the package because the
code has no stated license, reproduces `r count_of(a, "PASS")` of the
`r nrow(a)` published counts
(`inst/validation/python/ref_gould2017_author_grid.csv`). The authors' code
itself, run by a script outside the package, gives
`r sum(ac$author_code == ac$published)` of the `r nrow(ac)` published counts
(`inst/validation/results/gould2017_author_code.csv`). The differences
from the exact counts of bssd come from the grids (100 values of \(R\) in
\((0, 10)\), with the threshold 2 evaluated at the grid point 1.98, for the
binomial model; a coarse grid of the expected control count for the Poisson
model). The binomial counts of
Table III were computed with the lognormal prior between 0.1 and 8, the
default of the authors' code, which is used here as well.

```{r table3, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(quantity = sub("^X_crit, ", "", t3$quantity),
                        published = t3$published, bssd = t3$reproduced,
                        judgement = t3$judgement), align = "lrrl")
```

## Numerical integration

```{r check, include = FALSE}
v <- read_results("validation", "validate_methods_python.csv")
vc <- v[grepl("^PY_CANARY", v$id), ]
j <- read_results("validation", "validate_jags_methods.csv")
jc <- j[grepl("^J2_CANARY", j$id), ]
```

For the binomial likelihood, the posterior is integrated over
\(\mathrm{logit}(p_c)\) by Gauss-Legendre quadrature, and for each of its
nodes over an interval of \(\log R\) (or \(p_d\)) located from the
conditional posterior; for the ratio the interval ends at the truncation
point \(R = 1 / p_c\), where the density of \(\log R\) can be largest
when many subjects had the event. Against independent Python computations
on dense grids split exactly at the thresholds, the largest absolute
difference of the `r nrow(vc)` compared quantities (five data sets: the
ratio, the difference, the odds ratio, the Poisson likelihood, and the
ratio when all 100 subjects had the event) is `r fmt_e(max(vc$abs_diff))`. For the Poisson
likelihood, MCMC in JAGS gives `r fmt(jc$reference[1])` for
\(P(R > 2 \mid X)\) against `r fmt(jc$bssd[1])` from bssd
(`r jc$judgement[1]`).

## References

Gould, A. L. and Wang, W. B. (2017). Monitoring potential adverse event rate
differences using data from blinded trials: the canary in the coal mine.
*Statistics in Medicine*, 36(1), 92--104. <https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.7129>
